## 10.5 On the Stack: 36-Bit Bases, Boolean Logic & Bitwise Workbench

Whether converting bases, rolling a 36-bit two's-complement odometer across zero, snapping an IPv4 address to its subnet boundary, packing RGB565 color channels, or cracking open an IEEE-754 floating-point word, you always start with a word in hand, cleave it at a power-of-two boundary $2^k$ into an upper quotient and a lower remainder, and recombine the pieces from the inside out. On the StackCalc SC-32, the Euclidean division key (`[↱] [÷R]`) performs that exact cleavage in a single keystroke—placing the upper quotient $\lfloor Y / X \rfloor$ in Register `X` and the lower remainder $Y \bmod X$ in Register `Y`—while `[↰] [BASE]` switches seamlessly among `[DEC]`, `[HEX]`, `[OCT]`, and `[BIN]` without ever disturbing the four stack registers (`T, Z, Y, X`). Let us step onto the workbench and put this 36-bit engine through its paces.

![Decimal 255 converted in place to hexadecimal FFh on the SC-32 transflective display while preserving all four stack registers.](../assets/manuals/screenshots/sc32_base_hex_logic.png)

### 10.5.1 Live Radix Lenses (`DEC`, `HEX`, `OCT`, `BIN`) & Direct Hex Entry

Following the classic HP-32SII philosophy, the SC-32 `[↰] [BASE]` menu (accessed via Left Shift `[↰]` on the multiplication key `[×]`, Row 5, Column 3) treats number bases as **live display and entry lenses** over the same underlying 36-bit registers:

| Base System | Keystroke | Screen Suffix | Allowed Character Digits | Example Formatted Display |
| :--- | :--- | :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **Decimal** | `[↰] [BASE] [DEC]` | *(none)* | `0` through `9` | `1042` |
| **Hexadecimal** | `[↰] [BASE] [HEX]` | `h` | `0` through `9`, `A` through `F` | `412h` |
| **Octal** | `[↰] [BASE] [OCT]` | `o` | `0` through `7` | `2022o` |
| **Binary** | `[↰] [BASE] [BIN]` | `b` | `0` and `1` | `10000010010b` |

Switching between base modes **never destroys, alters, or shifts the values in the operational stack ($X, Y, Z, T$)**. If Register $X$ holds `255` in Decimal mode, pressing `[↰] [BASE] [HEX]` instantly re-renders the register as `FFh`, pressing `[↰] [BASE] [OCT]` shows `377o`, and pressing `[↰] [BASE] [BIN]` reveals all eight asserted bits as `11111111b`.

When Hexadecimal mode (`[HEX]`) is active, the top row of primary scientific keys (Row 1, Columns 0 through 5) maps directly to the printed alpha legends $A$ through $F$: `[√x]` enters $\mathbf{A}$ ($10_{10}$), `[eˣ]` enters $\mathbf{B}$ ($11_{10}$), `[LN]` enters $\mathbf{C}$ ($12_{10}$), `[yˣ]` enters $\mathbf{D}$ ($13_{10}$), `[1/x]` enters $\mathbf{E}$ ($14_{10}$), and `[Σ+]` enters $\mathbf{F}$ ($15_{10}$). To enter the classic debugging magic number `0xDEADBEEF`, simply key `[yˣ] [1/x] [√x] [yˣ] [eˣ] [1/x] [1/x] [Σ+]`. *(In the workbench tables below, hexadecimal literals such as `C0A80A2D` or `1F` are written in compact hex notation for readability; on the physical keypad in `[HEX]` mode, always enter the hex digits `A`–`F` using that top row `[√x]`–`[Σ+]`.)* Whenever you want to apply scientific functions (`[√x]`, `[LN]`, `[yˣ]`) to a hexadecimal value, switch back to Decimal mode (`[↰] [BASE] [DEC]`) first so the top-row keys resume their mathematical roles.

Because the SC-32 preserves all four stack registers across base changes, you can also mix radices right in the middle of a calculation without jotting down a single intermediate number: to add a hexadecimal base offset $3\text{A}7_{16}$ to an octal permission mask $452_8$ and read the sum in decimal, switch to Hex (`[↰] [BASE] [HEX]`) and enter `3 [√x] 7 [ENTER]` ($3\text{A}7_{16} = 935_{10}$), switch directly to Octal (`[↰] [BASE] [OCT]`) and add `452 [+]` ($2261_8$), and then switch to Decimal (`[↰] [BASE] [DEC]`) to read the combined total **$1,201_{10}$** in Register $X$.

### 10.5.2 Euclidean Remainder Extraction (`÷R`) & IPv4 Subnet Partitioning

Suppose a DMA controller accesses byte offset $12,345$ inside a flash memory array organized into 16-byte rows ($N = Q \cdot D + R$). Working in decimal (`[DEC]`) mode, keying `12345 [ENTER] 16 [↱] [÷R]` computes $12,345 \div 16$ with simultaneous quotient and remainder, placing the whole quotient $Q = \mathbf{771}$ (the 16-byte row index) in Register $X$ and the remainder $R = 12345 \bmod 16 = \mathbf{771}$ (the byte offset within row $771$) in Register $Y$:

| Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | What Happens on the Stack |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| `12345 [ENTER]` | 0 | 0 | 12345 | 12345 | Load integer dividend $12,345$ |
| `16 [↱] [÷R]` | 0 | 0 | **9** | **771** | Quotient $Q=771$ in Register X, remainder $R=9$ in Register Y |
| `[x⇄y]` | 0 | 0 | 771 | **9** | Swap registers to access remainder $9$ directly |

Now apply that exact `[↱] [÷R]` split to an IPv4 packet addressed to final host octet `205` on a `/28` VLAN interface (`255.255.255.240`, block stride $2^{32-28} = 16$). Working in `[DEC]` mode, keying `205 [ENTER] 16 [↱] [÷R] 16 [×]` divides `205` by `16` via `[↱] [÷R]` (placing block index `12` in Register $X$ and host offset `13` in Register $Y$) and multiplies by `16` to snap directly to the aligned `/28` subnet boundary **`192`**:

| Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | What Happens on the Stack |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| `205` | 0 | 0 | 0 | 205 | Enter final host octet `205` |
| `[ENTER]` | 0 | 0 | 205 | 205 | Stage `205` in Register Y |
| `16 [↱] [÷R]` | 0 | 0 | 13 | 12 | Cleave at stride $16$: block `12` in X, host offset `13` in Y |
| `16 [×]` | 0 | 0 | 13 | 192 | Multiply by $16$ for aligned `/28` network ID `192` |

To partition a full 32-bit IPv4 workstation address `192.168.10.45` (`C0A80A2Dh`) on a `/24` subnet ($2^{32-24} = 2^8 = 256_{10} = \text{100h}$), switch to `[HEX]` mode and execute three steps:
* **Extract the `/24` Network Base Address:** Keying `C0A80A2D [ENTER] 100 [↱] [÷R] 100 [×]` cleaves and aligns the `/24` network address **`C0A80A00h`** (`192.168.10.0`) while leaving the host offset (`2Dh`) in Register $Y$.
* **Isolate the Host Wildcard Mask:** Subtracting the `/24` netmask from the all-ones broadcast word via `FFFFFFFF [ENTER] FFFFFF00 [-]` isolates the 8-bit wildcard mask **`FFh`** (`0.0.0.255`).
* **Compute the Subnet Broadcast Address:** Adding that wildcard mask to the aligned network address via `C0A80A00 [ENTER] FF [+]` produces the `/24` broadcast address **`C0A80AFFh`** (`192.168.10.255`):

| Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | What Happens on the Stack |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| `C0A80A2D` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `C0A80A2Dh` | Enter packed 32-bit IPv4 address `192.168.10.45` |
| `[ENTER]` | `0h` | `0h` | `C0A80A2Dh` | `C0A80A2Dh` | Duplicate address into Register Y |
| `100 [↱] [÷R]` | `0h` | `0h` | `2Dh` | `C0A80Ah` | Split `/24` prefix `C0A80Ah` into X and host `2Dh` into Y |
| `100 [×]` | `0h` | `0h` | `2Dh` | `C0A80A00h` | Align `/24` network base address `192.168.10.0` |
| `FF [+]` | `0h` | `0h` | `2Dh` | `C0A80AFFh` | Add host wildcard `FFh` for broadcast `192.168.10.255` |

### 10.5.3 36-Bit Two's Complement Odometer Seams & Hardware Bit-Fields

We can inspect the two rollover seams of the 36-bit two's complement odometer directly on the stack in `[HEX]` mode:
* **Signed Positive Overflow Seam (`+Max + 1 → -Min`):** Load the largest positive signed 36-bit integer `7FFFFFFFFh` ($+2^{35} - 1 = +34,359,738,367_{10}$) and add `1` via `7FFFFFFFF [ENTER] 1 [+]` to roll across the sign boundary to **`800000000h`** ($-34,359,738,368_{10}$).
* **Zero Underflow Seam (`0 - 1 → -1`):** Start at `0` and subtract `1` via `0 [ENTER] 1 [-]` to roll backward across zero to **`FFFFFFFFFh`** ($-1_{10}$, all 36 bits asserted):

| Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | What Happens on the Stack |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| `7FFFFFFFF [ENTER]` | `0h` | `0h` | `7FFFFFFFFh` | `7FFFFFFFFh` | Load maximum signed positive 36-bit bound |
| `1 [+]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | **`800000000h`** | Overflow rolls over to minimum negative bound |
| `0 [ENTER] 1 [-]` | `0h` | `0h` | `800000000h` | **`FFFFFFFFFh`** | Underflow to $-1_{10}$; all 36 bits set (`FFFFFFFFFh`) |

Every bit-field shift and mask operation maps directly to a power of two $M = 2^k$ *([Shannon, 1938](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-shannon1938))*:

| Bit-Field / Masking Operation | Mathematical Equivalent ($M = 2^k$) | SC-32 RPN Keystrokes (`HEX` / `DEC`) | Result Location |
| :--- | :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **Left Shift ($X \ll k$)** | $X \times 2^k$ | `X [ENTER] M [×]` | Shifted word in **`X`** |
| **Right Shift ($X \gg k$)** | $\lfloor X / 2^k \rfloor$ | `X [ENTER] M [↱] [÷R]` (or `[÷]` in `HEX`/`OCT`/`BIN`) | Upper bits in **`X`** |
| **Low-Bit Mask ($X \ \& \ (2^k - 1)$)** | $X \bmod 2^k$ | `X [ENTER] M [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y]` | Low $k$ bits in **`X`** |
| **High-Bit Alignment ($X \ \& \ \sim(2^k - 1)$)** | $\lfloor X / 2^k \rfloor \times 2^k$ | `X [ENTER] M [↱] [÷R] M [×]` | Aligned base in **`X`** |
| **Set Disjoint Bit $k$** | $X + 2^k$ | `X [ENTER] M [+]` | Updated word in **`X`** |
| **Clear Set Bit $k$** | $X - 2^k$ | `X [ENTER] M [-]` | Updated word in **`X`** |
| **32-Bit Unsigned Complement** | $\text{FFFFFFFF}_{16} - X$ | `FFFFFFFF [ENTER] X [-]` | Inverted mask in **`X`** |

*(Note that for right bit-shifts in `[DEC]` mode, `[↱] [÷R]` is preferred over `[÷]` because `[÷]` retains fractional decimal digits in Decimal mode, whereas `[↱] [÷R]` always truncates directly to the integer quotient $\lfloor X / 2^k \rfloor$ in every base!)*

Suppose a 32-bit GPIO direction register (`GPIO_DIR`) holds `0x00001804` (Pins 2, 11, and 12 configured as outputs, Pin 5 currently `0`). To set Pin 5 ($2^5 = 32_{10} = \text{20h}$) in `[HEX]` mode, keying `1804 [ENTER] 20 [+]` produces **`1824h`**:

| Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | What Happens on the Stack |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| `1804` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `1804h` | Enter current `GPIO_DIR` register value `1804h` |
| `[ENTER]` | `0h` | `0h` | `1804h` | `1804h` | Stage `1804h` in Register Y |
| `20` | `0h` | `0h` | `1804h` | `20h` | Enter Bit 5 positional weight $2^5 = \text{20h}$ |
| `[+]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `1824h` | Assert Bit 5 without carry (`1824h`) |

Similarly, if a port output register holds `0x00000017` ($0001\,0111_2$) with a heartbeat line on Bit 2 ($2^2 = \text{4h}$), working in `[HEX]` mode lets us toggle and audit individual status bits without disturbing neighboring pins:
* **Clear & Restore a Heartbeat Pin:** Keying `17 [ENTER] 4 [-]` clears Bit 2 to produce **`13h`**, and adding `4` back via `13 [ENTER] 4 [+]` (or `[↰] [LASTX] [+]`) restores **`17h`**.
* **Spacecraft Telemetry Fault Mask (`XOR` via Borrow-Free Subtraction):** When comparing a spacecraft downlink status word `0x5F5A` against a nominal baseline mask `0x5A50` whose asserted bits are a subset of the active word (so that subtracting `5A50h` triggers zero column borrows and acts identically to bitwise `XOR`), keying `5F5A [ENTER] 5A50 [-]` in `[HEX]` mode isolates the newly tripped fault-bit mask **`50Ah`** ($\mathbf{10100001010\text{b}}$ in `[BIN]`, revealing a Hamming weight of **$4\text{ bits}$** at positions 1, 3, 8, and 10).

To extract a middle bit-field—such as Bits [7:4] (`6h`) from a 16-bit ADC configuration register holding `0x3C6A`—work in `[HEX]` mode in two steps:
* **Step 1 — Strip Upper Byte (`mod 100h`):** Key `3C6A [ENTER] 100 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y]` to isolate the lower 8-bit byte **`6Ah`**.
* **Step 2 — Shift Right by 4 Bits (`÷ 10h`):** Divide by $2^4 = \text{10h}$ via `6A [ENTER] 10 [÷]` to isolate Bits [7:4] = **`6h`**:

| Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | What Happens on the Stack |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| `3C6A [ENTER]` | `0h` | `0h` | `3C6Ah` | `3C6Ah` | Stage 16-bit ADC register word `3C6Ah` |
| `100 [↱] [÷R]` | `0h` | `0h` | `6Ah` | `3Ch` | Split upper byte `3Ch` into X and lower byte `6Ah` into Y |
| `[x⇄y]` | `0h` | `0h` | `3Ch` | `6Ah` | Swap lower byte `6Ah` (Bits [7:0]) into Register X |
| `10 [÷]` | `0h` | `0h` | `3Ch` | `6h` | Shift right by 4 bits (`÷ 10h`) to isolate Bits [7:4] = `6h` |

### 10.5.4 Packing RGB565 Pixels, Slicing Base64 Sextets & Reversing Endianness

Let us now pack 5-bit Red (`1Fh`), 6-bit Green (`15h`), and 5-bit Blue (`06h`) into a single 16-bit `RGB565` display word in `[HEX]` mode:
* **Shift Red into Bits [15:11]:** Multiply `1Fh` by $2^{11} = 800\text{h}$ via `1F [ENTER] 800 [×]` to obtain **`F800h`**.
* **Shift Green into Bits [10:5]:** Multiply `15h` by $2^5 = 20\text{h}$ via `15 [ENTER] 20 [×]` to obtain **`2A0h`**, and press `[+]` to merge Red and Green (`FAA0h`).
* **Add Blue in Bits [4:0]:** Add `06h` via `FAA0 [ENTER] 6 [+]` to complete the packed 16-bit pixel word **`FAA6h`**:

| Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | What Happens on the Stack |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| `1F [ENTER]` | `0h` | `0h` | `1Fh` | `1Fh` | Stage 5-bit Red channel `1Fh` ($31_{10}$) |
| `800 [×]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `F800h` | Shift Red left 11 bits (`× 800h`) into Bits [15:11] |
| `15 [ENTER]` | `0h` | `F800h` | `15h` | `15h` | Stage 6-bit Green channel `15h` ($21_{10}$); Red lifts to Z |
| `20 [×]` | `0h` | `0h` | `F800h` | `2A0h` | Shift Green left 5 bits (`× 20h`) into Bits [10:5] |
| `[+]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `FAA0h` | Combine shifted Red and Green channels (`FAA0h`) |
| `6 [+]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `FAA6h` | Add 5-bit Blue channel `06h` for packed `RGB565` word `FAA6h` |

Conversely, given a packed 16-bit RGB565 pixel `0xF38E` in `[HEX]` mode, keying `F38E [ENTER] 800 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 20 [↱] [÷R]` unpacks all three color channels onto the visible stack in one pass: Red in Register $Z$ (`1Eh` $= 30_{10}$), Green in Register $X$ (`1Ch` $= 28_{10}$), and Blue in Register $Y$ (`Eh` $= 14_{10}$).

In the same way, to slice the 24-bit ASCII string `"Man"` (`4D616Eh`) into four 6-bit Base64 sextet indices in `[HEX]` mode using divisors $2^{18} = \text{40000h}$, $2^{12} = \text{1000h}$, and $2^6 = \text{40h}$:
* **Sextet 1 (Bits [23:18]):** Keying `4D616E [ENTER] 40000 [÷]` extracts **`13h`** ($19_{10} \implies$ Base64 `'T'`).
* **Sextet 2 (Bits [17:12]):** Keying `4D616E [ENTER] 40000 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 1000 [÷]` extracts **`16h`** ($22_{10} \implies$ Base64 `'W'`).
* **Sextet 3 (Bits [11:6]):** Keying `4D616E [ENTER] 1000 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 40 [÷]` extracts **`5h`** ($5_{10} \implies$ Base64 `'F'`).
* **Sextet 4 (Bits [5:0]):** Keying `4D616E [ENTER] 40 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y]` extracts **`2Eh`** ($46_{10} \implies$ Base64 `'u'`), confirming that `"Man"` encodes to **`TWFu`**:

| Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | What Happens on the Stack |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| `4D616E [ENTER] 40000 [÷]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | **`13h`** | Sextet 1: `4D616Eh >> 18 = 13h` ($19_{10} \implies \mathbf{T}$) |
| `4D616E [ENTER] 40000 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 1000 [÷]` | `13h` | `13h` | `13h` | **`16h`** | Sextet 2: remainder `>> 12 = 16h` ($22_{10} \implies \mathbf{W}$) |
| `4D616E [ENTER] 1000 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 40 [÷]` | `16h` | `16h` | `4D6h` | **`5h`** | Sextet 3: remainder `>> 6 = 5h` ($5_{10} \implies \mathbf{F}$) |
| `4D616E [ENTER] 40 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y]` | `4D6h` | `5h` | `13585h` | **`2Eh`** | Sextet 4: lower 6-bit remainder = `2Eh` ($46_{10} \implies \mathbf{u}$) |

*(Single-Entry `÷R` Cascade: Chaining `4D616E [ENTER] 40000 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 1000 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 40 [↱] [÷R]` unpacks all four Base64 indices across the four stack registers—`13h` in $T$, `16h` in $Z$, `2Eh` in $Y$, and `5h` in $X$—with `4D616E` keyed only once.)*

When converting a 4-byte Big-Endian network word `0x12345678` into Little-Endian byte order `0x78563412` in `[HEX]` mode, we isolate each byte and shift it to its mirrored lane before summing with `[+] [+] [+]`:
* **Byte 0 $\to$ Byte 3:** Shift `78h` left 24 bits via `12345678 [ENTER] 100 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 1000000 [×]` $\rightarrow$ **`78000000h`**.
* **Byte 1 $\to$ Byte 2:** Shift `56h` left 16 bits via `12345678 [ENTER] 10000 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 100 [↱] [÷R] 10000 [×]` $\rightarrow$ **`560000h`**.
* **Byte 2 $\to$ Byte 1:** Shift `34h` left 8 bits via `12345678 [ENTER] 1000000 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 10000 [↱] [÷R] 100 [×]` $\rightarrow$ **`3400h`**.
* **Byte 3 $\to$ Byte 0:** Extract MSB `12h` via `12345678 [ENTER] 1000000 [÷]` $\rightarrow$ **`12h`**, and sum all four lanes into **`78563412h`**:

| Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | What Happens on the Stack |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| `78 [ENTER] 1000000 [×]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `78000000h` | Shift LSB `78h` left 24 bits into Byte 3 (`78000000h`) |
| `56 [ENTER] 10000 [×]` | `0h` | `0h` | `78000000h` | `560000h` | Shift `56h` left 16 bits into Byte 2 (`560000h`) |
| `[+]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `78560000h` | Merge Bytes 3 and 2 (`78560000h`) |
| `34 [ENTER] 100 [×]` | `0h` | `0h` | `78560000h` | `3400h` | Shift `34h` left 8 bits into Byte 1 (`3400h`) |
| `[+]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `78563400h` | Merge Bytes 3, 2, and 1 (`78563400h`) |
| `12` | `0h` | `0h` | `78563400h` | `12h` | Enter MSB `12h` into Byte 0 position |
| `[+]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `78563412h` | Complete Little-Endian word `78563412h` |

### 10.5.5 RFC 1071 Checksums, Circular Rotations (`ROL`), UART Dividers & IEEE-754 Unpacking

Suppose summing the 16-bit words of an IPv4 packet header in a 32-bit accumulator yields $\text{Header Sum} = 2653\text{D}_{16}$. In `[HEX]` mode, loading `2653D [ENTER]` and dividing by $2^{16} = \text{10000h}$ via `10000 [↱] [÷R]` places the upper carry (`2h`) in Register $X$ and the lower 16 bits (`653Dh`) in Register $Y$; pressing `[+]` folds the end-around carry (`653Fh`), and subtracting from `FFFFh` via `FFFF [x⇄y] [-]` yields the one's-complement wire checksum **`9AC0h`** ($39,616_{10}$ in `[DEC]`):

| Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | What Happens on the Stack |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| `2653D [ENTER]` | `0h` | `0h` | `2653Dh` | `2653Dh` | Load 32-bit accumulated IPv4 header sum `2653Dh` |
| `10000 [↱] [÷R]` | `0h` | `0h` | `653Dh` | `2h` | Split upper 16-bit carry `2h` into X and low word `653Dh` into Y |
| `[+]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `653Fh` | Fold end-around carry into 16-bit sum (`653Fh`) |
| `FFFF` | `0h` | `0h` | `653Fh` | `FFFFh` | Stage all-ones 16-bit mask `FFFFh` |
| `[x⇄y]` | `0h` | `0h` | `FFFFh` | `653Fh` | Swap folded sum into X beneath `FFFFh` in Y |
| `[-]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `9AC0h` | One's-complement RFC 1071 header checksum `9AC0h` |

Similarly, to execute a circular 1-bit left rotation (`ROL 1`) on the 8-bit byte `0x85` ($10000101_2 \implies 00001011_2 = \text{0Bh}$) in `[HEX]` mode at the 8-bit boundary $2^8 = \text{100h}$:
* **Step 1 — Shift Left by 1 Bit:** Double the byte via `85 [ENTER] 2 [×]` to obtain **`10Ah`**.
* **Step 2 — Split Overflow Carry at `100h`:** Cleave the 8-bit remainder (`0Ah` in $Y$) and overflow carry (`1h` in $X$) via `10A [ENTER] 100 [↱] [÷R]` ($\rightarrow$ **`1h`**).
* **Step 3 — Fold Carry into LSB:** Add the carry bit back into Bit 0 via `10A [ENTER] 100 [↱] [÷R] [+]` to complete the rotated byte **`Bh`**:

| Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | What Happens on the Stack |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| `85 [ENTER] 2 [×]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | **`10Ah`** | Shift byte left by 1 bit ($85\text{h} \times 2 = 10\text{Ah}$) |
| `100 [↱] [÷R]` | `0h` | `0h` | `Ah` | **`1h`** | Extract carry bit ($X=1\text{h}$) and rotated byte ($Y=\text{Ah}$) |
| `[+]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | **`Bh`** | Add carry bit into LSB: $10\text{Ah} \bmod 100\text{h} + 1\text{h} = \text{Ah} + 1\text{h} = \text{Bh}$ |

To configure a UART baud-rate divider from a $f_{\text{clk}} = 150.0\text{ MHz}$ peripheral clock at $115,200\text{ baud}$ with $8\times$ oversampling ($\text{Divider} = \frac{150,000,000}{8 \times 115,200} \approx 162.760417$), switch to `[DEC]` mode. Keying `150000000 [ENTER] 8 [÷] 115200 [÷]` evaluates the exact floating-point baud divider **`162.760416667`**, and `[IP]` / `[FP]` split out the 16-bit integer register (`IBRD = 162`) and 6-bit sixty-fourths fractional register (`FBRD = 49`):

| Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | What Happens on the Stack |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| `150000000` | $0.00000000$ | $0.00000000$ | $0.00000000$ | $150000000.$ | Enter $150\text{ MHz}$ peripheral clock frequency |
| `[ENTER]` | $0.00000000$ | $0.00000000$ | $150000000.$ | $150000000.$ | Stage clock frequency in Register Y |
| `8 [÷]` | $0.00000000$ | $0.00000000$ | $0.00000000$ | $18750000.0$ | Divide by $8\times$ oversampling factor |
| `115200 [÷]` | $0.00000000$ | $0.00000000$ | $0.00000000$ | $162.760417$ | Exact baud divider $162.760417$ |
| `[ENTER]` | $0.00000000$ | $0.00000000$ | $162.760417$ | $162.760417$ | Duplicate baud divider into Register Y |
| `[IP]` | $0.00000000$ | $0.00000000$ | $162.760417$ | $162.000000$ | Extract integer baud register `IBRD = 162` |
| `[x⇄y] [FP]` | $0.00000000$ | $0.00000000$ | $162.000000$ | $0.76041667$ | Swap and extract fractional remainder $0.760417$ |
| `64 [×]` | $0.00000000$ | $0.00000000$ | $162.000000$ | $48.6666667$ | Scale fraction into sixty-fourths ($48.67 / 64$) |
| `[↰] [RND]` | $0.00000000$ | $0.00000000$ | $162.000000$ | $49.0000000$ | Round to nearest integer for `FBRD = 49` |

Finally, to unpack the 32-bit IEEE-754 single-precision word `0xC0C80000` ($-6.25_{10}$) in `[HEX]` mode, chain two `[↱] [÷R]` divisions—first by $2^{23} = \text{800000h}$ and then by $2^8 = \text{100h}$—to place the 23-bit mantissa (`480000h`) in Register $Z$, the 8-bit biased exponent (`81h` $= 129_{10}$) in Register $Y$, and the 1-bit sign (`1h`) in Register $X$:

| Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | What Happens on the Stack |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| `C0C80000 [ENTER]` | `0h` | `0h` | `C0C80000h` | `C0C80000h` | Stage 32-bit IEEE-754 float word `C0C80000h` |
| `800000 [↱] [÷R]` | `0h` | `0h` | `480000h` | `181h` | Cleave at Bit 23: mantissa `480000h` in Y, upper 9 bits `181h` in X |
| `100 [↱] [÷R]` | `0h` | `480000h` | `81h` | `1h` | Cleave at Bit 8: Sign `1h` in X, Exponent `81h` in Y, Mantissa in Z |
| `[↰] [BASE] [DEC]` | 0 | 4718592 | 129 | 1 | Switch to Decimal: $S = 1$, $E = 129$, $M = 4,718,592$ |
| `[x⇄y] 127 [-]` | 4718592 | 4718592 | 1 | 2 | Subtract bias $127$ to reveal true binary exponent $e = 2$ |

Similarly, for a 64-bit IEEE-754 double-precision float (`binary64`) such as $-13.375_{10}$ (`0xC02AC00000000000`, upper 32-bit word `0xC02AC000`), chaining `C02AC000 [ENTER] 100000 [↱] [÷R] 800 [↱] [÷R]` in `[HEX]` mode cleaves at $2^{20} = \text{100000h}$ and $2^{11} = \text{800h}$ to leave Sign $S = \mathbf{1}$ (`1h`) in $X$, Biased Exponent $E = \mathbf{\text{402h}}$ ($1026_{10} \implies e = 1026 - 1023 = \mathbf{3}$) in $Y$, and upper 20-bit significand `AC000h` ($\frac{704,512}{2^{20}} = 0.671875$) in $Z$, reconstructing $(-1)^1 \times 2^3 \times (1 + 0.671875) = \mathbf{-13.375}$.

### 10.5.6 Combinatorics (PROB) & Birthday Paradox Collision Probability

Switching back to `[DEC]` mode, let us evaluate discrete state spaces and collision probabilities using the **`[↱] [PROB]` menu** (`Right Shift [↱] above [eˣ]`):
* **RAID Parity Groups vs. Failover Chains (`[Cn,r]` & `[Pn,r]`):** To count how many ways a 12-drive storage array can select $5$ drives for a RAID parity group ($C(12, 5)$) versus an ordered 5-drive failover chain ($P(12, 5)$), key `12 [ENTER] 5 [↱] [PROB] [Cn,r]` to obtain **`792`** unordered subsets, or `12 [ENTER] 5 [↱] [PROB] [Pn,r]` to obtain **`95,040`** ordered sequences.
* **Hexadecimal Pipeline Permutations ($P(16, 4)$):** Choosing an ordered 4-nibble hexadecimal sequence without repetition from $16$ hex digits via `16 [ENTER] 4 [↱] [PROB] [Pn,r]` yields **`43,680`**.
* **Full-Mesh Router Topology ($C(7, 2)$):** Wiring a full mesh of point-to-point links among $7$ network routers via `7 [ENTER] 2 [↱] [PROB] [Cn,r]` requires **`21`** cables.
* **Packet-Queue Factorial Permutations ($15!$):** Permuting $15$ packet-routing priorities via `15 [↱] [PROB] [↰] [x!]` spans **`1,307,674,368,000`** states ($12! = 479,001,600$ for $12$ items).
* **The 23-Person Birthday Collision Paradox ($1 - P(365, 23)/365^{23}$):** Keying `365 [ENTER] 23 [↱] [PROB] [Pn,r]` computes the number of collision-free birthday assignments across $23$ people ($4.220082 \times 10^{58}$), dividing by `365 [ENTER] 23 [yˣ] [÷]` gives the no-collision probability $P_{\text{unique}} = \mathbf{0.492703}$, and subtracting from $1$ via `1 [x⇄y] [-]` confirms that the probability of a shared birthday or hash collision is already **`0.507297`** (**$50.73\%$**)!

### 10.5.7 From Binary Registers to the Mathematics of Time and Money

Stepping back from Claude Shannon's relay circuits and our 36-bit two's-complement odometer, notice the quiet mathematical thread that tied every base conversion and bit-packing problem together: **positional power scaling**. Writing a number in base $b$ means weighting each column by a power $b^k$ and evaluating the resulting polynomial from the inside out—whether $b = 2$ inside a silicon logic gate, $b = 16$ inside a memory address map, or $b = 10$ on an everyday ledger. By giving you one-tap radix switching (`[HEX]`, `[DEC]`, `[OCT]`, `[BIN]`), two's-complement negation (`[+/-]`), and single-keystroke bit-field cleaving (`[↱] [÷R]`), the SC-32 lets you step inside the machine's native binary architecture without ever leaving the four-register stack.

From the silent binary hardware inside the calculator, we now return to everyday human life. Where do the exponential growth laws of Chapter 3, the Horner polynomial nesting of Chapter 7, and the root-finding engines of numerical analysis touch every household, student loan, homebuyer, and business on Earth? When we replace the discrete integer base $2$ with the compounding growth factor $(1 + i)$, positional power scaling across bit columns becomes **discounting and compounding across time**. We open that eight-hundred-year-old financial engine next in **[Chapter 11: The Eight-Hundred-Year Engine of Compound Interest: Time Value of Money](sc32/11-financial-tvm.md)**.

# Chapter 11: The Eight-Hundred-Year Engine of Compound Interest: Time Value of Money

## 11.1 Fibonacci's Merchants, The Percentage Asymmetry Trap & The Rule of 72

In the year 1202, a thirty-two-year-old Italian merchant's son named **Leonardo Pisano**—known to posterity as **Fibonacci**—returned to Pisa from the bustling Mediterranean ports of Bugia (in modern-day Algeria), Alexandria, and Constantinople. His father, Guglielmo Bonacci, had served as a customs official representing Pisan traders across North Africa, and young Leonardo had grown up watching Arab and North African mathematicians calculate with the nine Hindu-Arabic numerals (`1` through `9`) and the symbol `zephirum` (`0`), while European counting houses were still struggling to multiply Roman numerals (`MCCIV`) on counting boards.

When Fibonacci published his landmark treatise ***Liber Abaci*** (*The Book of Calculation*) in 1202, modern readers often assume it was a book about his famous breeding rabbits. In fact, the rabbit puzzle occupied barely half a page. Fibonacci filled the longest, most ambitious chapters of *Liber Abaci* with the real mathematical problem that kept twelfth-century Venetian, Genovese, and Pisan sea captains awake at night: **how do you compare a gold bezant in your hand today against a stream of payments arriving across different years in the future?**

Four centuries later, in 1613 London—just one year before John Napier unveiled his logarithms in Edinburgh—an English mathematician named **Richard Witt** published *Arithmeticall Questions, Touching the Buying or Exchange of Annuities*, the first comprehensive volume of compound-interest tables in the English language. Witt showed London merchants, landlords, and actuaries that **time acts like a geometric lens on money**: every year that a sum of capital $PV$ is put to work at periodic interest rate $i$, it is multiplied by the growth factor $(1 + i)$. Conversely, every year you have to wait in the future to receive a promised payment $FV$, its value today is *divided* by $(1 + i)$.

Whether you are a high-school student opening your first savings account, a college graduate comparing student loan repayment plans, a family signing a 30-year home mortgage, or a chief financial officer valuing a power plant, money is stored human time and labor. Understanding how percentages, compounding, and discounting work from the inside out is the single most practical mathematical skill of adult life.

### 11.1.1 Why a 20% Loss Followed by a 20% Gain Leaves You Poorer: The Percentage Asymmetry Trap

Before we step into multi-year compound interest, let us expose a deceptively simple percentage illusion that fools millions of investors, shoppers, and business owners every day.

Suppose you invest $\$100.00$ in a stock index fund. During a turbulent autumn, the market **drops by $20\%$**. The next spring, the market rallies and **gains $20\%$**. Are you back to even at $\$100.00$?

Human intuition—trained since childhood on symmetric addition and subtraction ($-20 + 20 = 0$)—almost always says *yes*. Yet trace what actually happens to your money step by step:

1. **The $20\%$ Drop:** Losing $20\%$ of $\$100.00$ subtracts $\$20.00$, shrinking your investment base to $\$100.00 \times (1 - 0.20) = \mathbf{\$80.00}$.
2. **The $20\%$ Gain:** When the market rebounds by $+20\%$, that $20\%$ gain is not applied to your original $\$100.00$—it is applied to your shrunken **$\$80.00$** base. Twenty percent of $\$80.00$ is only $+\$16.00$, bringing your account to $\$80.00 \times (1 + 0.20) = \mathbf{\$96.00}$.

You are still down **$-4.0\%$**. And what if your stock drops by **$50\%$** (from $\$100$ down to $\$50$)? A $+50\%$ gain on $\$50$ only brings you back to $\$75$; to recover from a $50\%$ loss back to $\$100$, you need a **+$100\%$ gain**!

Why do equal percentage losses and gains never cancel out? Because percentages combine **multiplicatively**, not additively. Recall the high-school algebra identity for the difference of two squares when a fractional drop $-x$ is followed by an equal fractional gain $+x$:

$$(1 - x)(1 + x) = 1 - x^2 < 1$$

Whenever $x > 0$, the product $(1 - x)(1 + x)$ is strictly less than $1$ by the penalty $x^2$ (for $x = 0.20$, the penalty is $x^2 = 0.20^2 = 0.04 = 4\%$). That exact multiplicative reality also explains two everyday commercial surprises:

- **Stacked Retail Markdowns:** When a store advertises *"30% seasonal sale, plus an extra 15% VIP coupon"* on a $\$280.00$ jacket, you do not get $30\% + 15\% = 45\%$ off. Instead, the $30\%$ markdown reduces $\$280.00$ to $\$280 \times 0.70 = \$196.00$, and the $15\%$ coupon takes $15\%$ off that $\$196.00$ sale price ($\$29.40$), leaving $\$196.00 \times 0.85 = \mathbf{\$166.60}$—an effective combined discount of $1 - (0.70)(0.85) = \mathbf{40.5\%}$.
- **The Markup vs. Gross Margin Trap:** Suppose a hardware startup builds a device for a landed cost of $C = \$60.00$, and the company's financial plan requires a **$40\%$ Gross Margin** (meaning $40\%$ of the final *selling price* must be gross profit). If a manager mistakenly adds a $40\%$ **markup** onto the $\$60.00$ cost ($\text{Price} = \$60 + 0.40 \times \$60 = \$84.00$), the profit is $\$24.00$ out of an $\$84.00$ selling price—which is only $\$24 / \$84 = \mathbf{28.57\%}$ gross margin. To achieve a true $40\%$ gross margin from the inside out, if profit accounts for $40\%$ of the selling price, then the $\$60.00$ manufacturing cost must represent the remaining $1 - 0.40 = 60\%$ ($0.60$) of the selling price:

$$\text{Selling Price} = \frac{\text{Cost}}{1 - \text{Gross Margin}} = \frac{\$60.00}{1 - 0.40} = \frac{\$60.00}{0.60} = \mathbf{\$100.00}$$

### 11.1.2 Why William Kahan Redesigned the Percentage Key—And How the Rule of 72 Works

Consider why so many people make mistakes with percentages: **every percentage only has meaning relative to its base amount**.

In 1979, UC Berkeley mathematician **William M. Kahan**—the chief architect of the IEEE-754 floating-point standard—published a celebrated analysis in the *Hewlett-Packard Journal* *([Kahan, 1979](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-kahan1979))* examining why conventional pocket calculators make percentage math so clumsy. On a typical algebraic calculator, if you want to add an $8.25\%$ sales tax to a $\$150.00$ invoice and you type `150 × 8.25 %`, the screen displays `12.38`—and **wipes out your original $\$150.00$ base amount**. To get the total invoice, you have to retype `+ 150 =` from scratch.

Kahan realized that in an inside-out stack architecture, a percentage key (`%`) should be **base-preserving**: when you have your base amount ($Y = 150.00$) on the second shelf and your percentage rate ($X = 8.25$) on the bottom shelf, pressing `%` should replace only the bottom shelf with the dollar tax ($X = 12.38$) while leaving your base amount ($Y = 150.00$) **untouched and visible right above it**. On the SC-32, the right-shifted **`[↱] [%]`** (Right Shift `[↱]` above `[COS]`) and **`[↱] [%CHG]`** (Right Shift `[↱]` above `[TAN]`) keys implement Kahan's base-preserving stack design directly: placing the base amount on Shelf $Y$ and the percentage on Shelf $X$ lets `[↱] [%]` compute the dollar adjustment on Shelf $X$ while keeping your original base intact on Shelf $Y$, ready for an immediate `[+]` (tax or markup) or `[-]` (discount).

What happens when a percentage rate $r\%$ is applied not once, but over and over again across $N$ years? Each year multiplies your balance by $(1 + r/100)$, turning addition into exponential growth:

$$FV = PV \left(1 + \frac{r}{100}\right)^N$$

How many years $N$ does it take for compound interest at an annual rate of $r\%$ to **double** your money ($FV / PV = 2$)? Taking the natural logarithm (from Chapter 3) of both sides:

$$\left(1 + \frac{r}{100}\right)^N = 2 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad N \ln\!\left(1 + \frac{r}{100}\right) = \ln 2 \approx 0.693147$$

As we saw in Chapter 3, for normal interest rates ($r \le 12\%$), the Taylor approximation $\ln(1 + r/100) \approx r/100$ gives $N \approx \frac{69.3}{r}$. And why did Franciscan friar **Luca Pacioli**—who first printed the rule in his monumental *Summa de arithmetica* (Venice, 1494)—and Renaissance merchants across Venice and Florence round $69.3$ slightly upward to **$72$** (allowing for the slight curvature of discrete annual compounding around $r \approx 8\%$)? Because **$72$ is divisible by $1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9,$ and $12$**, giving you the famous mental **Rule of 72**:

$$\text{Doubling Time (Years)} \approx \frac{72}{\text{Annual Interest Rate } r\%}$$

At $6\%$ annual return, your money doubles in about $72 / 6 = \mathbf{12\text{ years}}$; at $8\%$, in $72 / 8 = \mathbf{9\text{ years}}$; at $9\%$, in $72 / 9 = \mathbf{8\text{ years}}$. Conversely, if inflation runs at $3.2\%$ per year for $20\text{ years}$, dividing $\$100,000$ of uninvested cash by $(1.032)^{20} \approx 1.8776$ shrinks its real purchasing power nearly in half, down to **$\$53,260.60$**.

## 11.2 The Master Equation of Time and Money—And the Mortgage Amortization Surprise

### 11.2.1 How a Geometric Series Builds the Five-Variable TVM Balance Law

In real life, we rarely deposit a single lump sum and walk away for thirty years. Usually, three flows of money interact across $N$ compounding periods at periodic interest rate $i$:

1. **$PV$ (Present Value):** The starting lump sum at time $t = 0$ (such as a $\$350,000$ home mortgage loan or an initial retirement balance).
2. **$PMT$ (Periodic Payment):** A steady stream of equal payments made at every period $k = 1, 2, \dots, N$ (such as a monthly mortgage check, car payment, or 401(k) contribution).
3. **$FV$ (Future Value):** The final balance left at the end of period $N$ ($0$ for a fully paid-off loan, or a target nest egg for retirement).

How do all five variables—$N, i, PV, PMT,$ and $FV$—fit into a single mathematical equation?

Think of the present moment ($t = 0$) as the balance fulcrum of a scale. Every payment $PMT$ that arrives $k$ periods in the future must be discounted back to today by dividing by $(1 + i)^k$, and the final balance $FV$ at period $N$ must be discounted by $(1 + i)^N$:

$$PV + \frac{PMT}{(1+i)^1} + \frac{PMT}{(1+i)^2} + \cdots + \frac{PMT}{(1+i)^N} + \frac{FV}{(1+i)^N} = 0$$

Examine that middle sum of $N$ discounted payments: it is a classic high-school **geometric series** with common ratio $q = (1 + i)^{-1}$. Using Euclid's formula for the sum of a finite geometric series, those $N$ terms collapse into a single closed-form expression called the **Annuity Present-Value Factor ($a_{\overline{N}|i}$)**:

$$\sum_{k=1}^{N} (1 + i)^{-k} = \frac{1 - (1 + i)^{-N}}{i} = a_{\overline{N}|i}$$

Substituting that closed form gives the **Master Five-Variable Time Value of Money (`TVM`) Equation**:

$$PV + PMT \left[ \frac{1 - (1 + i)^{-N}}{i} \right] + FV (1 + i)^{-N} = 0$$

*(For an **Annuity Due**—such as an apartment lease or tuition payment where each check is paid at the **beginning** of the period rather than the end—each payment earns one extra period of compounding, multiplying the $PMT$ bracket by $(1 + i)$.)*

On the SC-32, pressing **`[↰] [TVM]`** (Left Shift `[↰]` above `[x∥y]`) maps the six top dynamic LFU softkeys (`[LFU0]`–`[LFU5]`) directly to **`N`** (`[N]`), **`I%`** (denoted `[I%YR]` in keystroke sequences as a reminder to enter the periodic interest rate per compounding interval), **`PV`** (`[PV]`), **`PMT`** (`[PMT]`), **`FV`** (`[FV]`), and **`END`/`BEG`** (`[LFU5]`, which toggles directly between Ordinary Annuity `END` and Annuity Due `BEG`). The five numerical softkeys obey a simple, deterministic **Store-vs.-Solve Rule**: *tapping a TVM softkey right after typing or calculating a number on the stack **stores** that value from Register $X$ into the TVM register; tapping a TVM softkey immediately after another TVM softkey **solves** for that unknown variable into Register $X$.*

### 11.2.2 Why Cash-Flow Sign Discipline Works Like Conservation of Energy

Why is the right-hand side of the Master TVM Equation equal to **zero**?

Because financial mathematics treats your wallet (or a company's treasury) exactly like a physical control volume in physics:
- **Cash Inflows ($+$) are Positive:** Any money flowing **into** your pocket (the $+\$350,000$ loan wire you receive from the bank when buying a house, or the $+\$1,000$ payout you receive when a bond matures) is entered with a **positive sign ($+$)**.
- **Cash Outflows ($-$) are Negative:** Any money flowing **out** of your pocket (the monthly mortgage check you mail to the bank, or the $-\$925.00$ purchase price you pay to buy a bond) is entered with a **negative sign ($-$)**.

When all cash inflows and outflows are discounted to the same point in time at the true interest rate $i$, **the net sum must balance to zero**. That physical sign rule immediately prevents confusion: if you receive a $+\$350,000$ mortgage loan today ($PV > 0$), your monthly repayments must flow *out* of your pocket ($PMT < 0$) to pay that debt down to $FV = 0$.

### 11.2.3 The 30-Year Mortgage Amortization Surprise: Why Month 237 Is the Turning Point

Let us walk through the most consequential calculation most families ever make: taking out a **30-year fixed-rate home mortgage**.

Suppose a family borrows **$PV = +\$350,000.00$** for 30 years (**$N = 30 \times 12 = 360\text{ months}$**, paid down to **$FV = \$0.00$**) at an annual interest rate of **$6.75\%$ APR**. Because payments occur monthly, the periodic interest rate per month is:

$$i = \frac{6.75\%}{12} = 0.5625\%\text{ per month} = 0.005625$$

Substituting $N = 360$ and $i = 0.005625$ into the Master TVM Equation fixes the required level monthly payment:

$$PMT = -PV \times \frac{i}{1 - (1 + i)^{-N}}$$

When we run this exact mortgage on the SC-32 workbench in the next section, we will see that the monthly check comes to nearly $\$2,300$—and that over thirty years, the family's $360$ payments total more than $\$817,000$, meaning they pay over $\$467,000$ in pure interest (more than $1.33$ times the original $\$350,000$ loan)!

Even more surprising is the hidden anatomy of **Month 1**. When the family mails their very first monthly check, how much of that payment actually reduces their $\$350,000$ loan balance?
- First, the bank charges one month's interest ($i = 0.5625\%$) on the entire starting principal ($I_1 = PV \times i$), which devours **$86.7\%$ of the Month 1 payment**.
- Only the tiny leftover sliver ($P_1 = |PMT| - I_1$, just **$13.3\%$ of the payment**) reduces the principal balance!

Why does it take until **Month 237**—nearly **twenty years** into a thirty-year mortgage—before at least half of your monthly check goes toward paying down your own house?

Because on any level-payment loan of $N$ periods at rate $i$, the principal portion $P_k$ of payment $k$ grows exponentially from the inside out according to $P_k = |PMT|(1 + i)^{-(N - k + 1)}$. Setting $P_k = \frac{1}{2}|PMT|$ shows that the **Amortization Crossover** occurs when $(1 + i)^{N - k + 1} = 2$—which is our exact **Rule of 72 doubling time** counted *backward from the end of the loan*. At $6.75\%$ APR ($i = 0.005625/\text{month}$), the doubling time is $\frac{\ln 2}{\ln(1.005625)} \approx 123.57\text{ months}$ ($\approx 10.3\text{ years}$) before Month $361$, landing right at Month $361 - 123.57 = \mathbf{237.43}$.

And that reveals a life-changing financial secret: **because early principal reduction is barely one-eighth of the monthly check, adding even a modest extra principal payment in the early years leaps forward along the exponential curve.** As we will verify to the exact cent on the stack below, adding just **$\$250.00\text{ per month}$** of extra principal nearly *doubles* the Month 1 principal reduction—eliminating more than **seven years of monthly payments** and saving over **$\$134,000$** in lifetime interest!

## 11.3 Valuing Future Cash Streams: Bonds, Net Present Value & Why IRR Needs a Root Solver

### 11.3.1 Why Bond Prices Move Opposite to Interest Rates

Step from the homeowner's kitchen table onto a bond trading desk. A **bond** is simply a tradable loan: when a corporation or government issues a 10-year, $\$1,000$ par-value bond with a $5.5\%$ annual coupon paid semi-annually ($N = 20$ six-month periods), the issuer promises to pay the bondholder **$PMT = +\$27.50$ every six months** for twenty periods, plus the **$FV = +\$1,000.00$ principal** at maturity.

Why does the market price ($PV$) of an existing bond **fall** whenever market interest rates **rise**?

Because the bond's future cash promises ($+\$27.50$ every six months and $+\$1,000$ at maturity) are printed in ink and cannot change. If new bonds in the market are suddenly paying $6.53\%$ annual yield ($3.2666\%$ per half-year), no investor will pay $\$1,000$ for your older $5.5\%$ bond unless you **discount its purchase price** down to **$PV = -\$925.00$**, so that the $\$75.00$ capital gain at maturity makes up for the lower semi-annual coupons. Because a bond is a level-coupon annuity plus a maturity redemption, the SC-32's `[↰] [TVM]` menu models bond prices (`[PV]`) and periodic yield (`I%`, denoted `[I%YR]`) in a single softkey tap.

In 1938, economist **Frederick Macaulay** asked a brilliant physical question about bonds: if a 3-year bond pays coupons at Year 1, Year 2, and Year 3 (plus principal at Year 3), what is the *effective waiting time* until you get your money back? Macaulay imagined placing weights along a horizontal beam at $t = 1, 2, 3\text{ years}$, where each weight equals the **present value** of that year's cash flow. The center-of-mass pivot point where that beam balances—identical in algebra to Archimedes' weighted centroid $\bar{x}_w = \frac{\sum t_k w_k}{\sum w_k}$ that we computed on the statistical bus in Chapter 6!—is **Macaulay Duration ($D$)**. Dividing by $(1 + y)$ gives **Modified Duration ($D^*$)**, which measures the exact percentage lever tilt in the bond's price for every $1\%$ shift in market interest rates:

$$\frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx -D^* \cdot \Delta y = -\frac{D}{1 + y} \cdot \Delta y$$

That mechanical seesaw explains why a 2-year Treasury note ($D^* \approx 1.9\text{ years}$) barely flinches when interest rates rise by $1\%$ ($\Delta P/P \approx -1.9\%$), whereas a 30-year zero-coupon bond—all of whose weight sits at the far end of a thirty-foot plank ($D = 30\text{ years}$)—plunges by nearly $30\%$ on the exact same rate hike!

### 11.3.2 Net Present Value (`NPV`) as a Horner Polynomial—And Why `IRR` Needs Richard Brent's Solver

What if an entrepreneur or corporate board is evaluating a factory, a solar array, or a software company whose future cash flows are **uneven**—say, generating free cash flows of $C_1 = \$10\text{M}$ in Year 1, $C_2 = \$12\text{M}$ in Year 2, $C_3 = \$15\text{M}$ in Year 3, and $C_4 = \$234\text{M}$ in Year 4 (operating cash flow plus terminal sale value), discounted at a $r = 10\%$ cost of capital?

Summing the present values of each year's cash flow gives the **Net Present Value (`NPV`)**:

$$\text{PV} = \frac{10}{1.10} + \frac{12}{1.10^2} + \frac{15}{1.10^3} + \frac{234}{1.10^4} = \mathbf{\$190.11\text{M}}$$

Viewed through the lens of **Chapter 7 (Polynomials & Root-Finding)**, if we write $x = 1 + r = 1.10$, discounting a stream of uneven cash flows is a **Horner polynomial in $1/x$**, peeled from the most distant year ($t = 4$) backward to the present ($t = 0$):

$$\text{PV} = \left(\left(\left(234 \div 1.10 + 15\right) \div 1.10 + 12\right) \div 1.10 + 10\right) \div 1.10$$

And that reveals a profound mathematical connection when we ask the inverse question: suppose a project costs $C_0 = -\$100,000$ upfront today and returns $C_1 = +\$30,000$, $C_2 = +\$40,000$, and $C_3 = +\$50,000$ over the next three years. What is the project's **Internal Rate of Return (`IRR`)**—the exact interest rate $r$ where the Net Present Value equals zero?

$$\text{NPV}(r) = -100,000 + \frac{30,000}{1+r} + \frac{40,000}{(1+r)^2} + \frac{50,000}{(1+r)^3} = 0$$

That equation reveals what we are really solving: finding the `IRR` (or finding the unknown periodic interest rate `I%` / `[I%YR]` on `[LFU1]` of a 30-year mortgage) is **finding the root of a polynomial of degree $N$**. As Niels Henrik Abel and Évariste Galois proved in Chapter 7, no algebraic radical formula exists when $N \ge 5$—and by **René Descartes's 1637 Rule of Signs**, a standard investment whose cash flows change sign only once ($-$ upfront, then $+, +, +$) is guaranteed to have a **unique positive root**, whereas a strip-mine or power-plant project that requires a large negative environmental cleanup outflow at the end ($-, +, +, -$) changes sign *twice* and can possess two distinct `IRR` roots! That is why the SC-32 pairs Horner evaluation on the 4-register stack with Richard Brent's **`[↱] [SOLVE]`** root-finder (and the 240-interval scan + bisection `[↰] [TVM]` engine across `N`, `I%`, `PV`, `PMT`, `FV`, and `END`/`BEG`) to model uneven `NPV` and `IRR` cash-flow streams right under its keys.

## 11.4 On the Stack: Percentages, Mortgages & TVM Cash-Flow Workbench

Across every financial problem we have explored—from Kahan's base-preserving percentages and markup-versus-margin pricing to 30-year mortgage amortization, bond duration, and Horner discounted cash flows—notice how naturally inside-out thinking protects you from financial illusions. In your mind, you keep your baseline principal or invoice amount on an upper shelf while evaluating the tax delta, growth ratio, or discount factor on the active shelf below. On the StackCalc SC-32, Register `Y` holds that preserved baseline while Register `X` computes `[↱] [%]` or `[↱] [%CHG]`, and the dedicated five-variable `[↰] [TVM]` menu (`[N]`, `[I%YR]`, `[PV]`, `[PMT]`, `[FV]`) links directly to the stack. Let us step onto the workbench and walk through each calculation keystroke by keystroke.

![The SC-32 transflective display executing multi-variable financial calculations with continuous stack preservation.](../assets/manuals/screenshots/sc32_tvm_mortgage.png)

### 11.4.1 Base-Preserving Percentages (`%`), Chain Discounts & Gross Margin Pricing

To format currency outputs rounded to cents while retaining full 64-bit internal precision, set the display mode to two decimal places (`[FIX] 2`) via `[↰] [DISP]` $\to$ `[FIX]` $\to$ `2` *([HP, 1982](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-hp15c1982))*. On the StackCalc SC-32, the **Percentage Function (`[↱] [%]`)** adheres strictly to William Kahan's non-destructive specification *([Kahan, 1979](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-kahan1979))*:

$$\text{Calculation: } \quad X \leftarrow \frac{Y \times X}{100}, \quad Y \leftarrow Y \text{ (Preserved)}, \quad \text{Lift} \leftarrow \text{TRUE}$$

On a $\$150.00$ consulting invoice at $8.25\%$ sales tax, keying `150 [ENTER] 8.25 [↱] [%]` places $\$12.38$ in Register $X$ while holding $\$150.00$ in Register $Y$, so pressing `[+]` yields $\$162.38$ in a single stroke. Similarly, keying `100 [ENTER] 8 [↱] [%]` on a $\$100.00$ baseline places the exact dollar amount ($\mathbf{8}$) in Register $X$ while freezing $100.00$ in Register $Y$.

For an enterprise server order subtotaling $\$18,450.00$ with $8.25\%$ state sales tax in `[FIX] 2` mode, keying `18450 [ENTER] 8.25 [↱] [%]` places the tax amount $X = \mathbf{\$1,522.13}$ below the preserved base $Y = \$18,450.00$, and pressing `[+]` sums the total invoice to **`$19,972.13`**:

| Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | What Happens on the Stack |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| `18450 [ENTER]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 18450.00 | 18450.00 | Stage pre-tax subtotal $\$18,450.00$ in Register Y |
| `8.25 [↱] [%]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 18450.00 | 1522.13 | Compute $8.25\%$ tax ($\$1,522.13$) in X; base preserved in Y |
| `[+]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 19972.13 | Add tax to preserved base for total invoice $\$19,972.13$ |

Base-preserving percentages streamline discounts and multi-step splits just as cleanly:
- **Single Volume Discount:** On an $\$85,000.00$ software license with a $17.5\%$ volume discount, keying `85000 [ENTER] 17.5 [↱] [%]` displays the dollar concession ($X = \mathbf{\$14,875.00}$) alongside the $\$85,000.00$ list price in $Y$, and pressing `[-]` yields the net invoice payable (**`$70,125.00`**).
- **Stacked Chain Markdowns:** For a $30\%$ seasonal sale followed by an extra $15\%$ VIP coupon on a $\$280.00$ jacket, keying `280 [ENTER] 30 [↱] [%]` followed by `[-]` deducts the first $30\%$ markdown $(\$84.00)$ to leave $\$196.00$ in Register $X$. Chaining `15 [↱] [%] [-]` then deducts the $15\%$ coupon $(\$29.40)$ against that reduced base to yield $\mathbf{\$166.60}$.
- **Shared vs. Itemized Bill Splitting:** To split an 8-person restaurant dinner bill of $\$480.00$ where 3 guests shared $\$96.00$ of wine while all 8 shared the food equally, deducting the wine tab via `480 [ENTER] 96 [-]` isolates the shared food bill $(\$384.00)$, and `8 [÷]` establishes the per-guest food share $(\$48.00)$. Computing the per-drinker wine share via `96 [ENTER] 3 [÷]` places $\$32.00$ in Register $X$ beneath $\$48.00$ in Register $Y$, so pressing `[+]` resolves the wine-drinker total ($X = \mathbf{\$80.00}$).

To compare the **Markup Trap** against true **Gross Margin Pricing** on a product with landed cost $C = \$60.00$ and target $40.0\%$ gross margin: adding a $40\%$ markup onto $\$60.00$ (`60 [ENTER] 40 [↱] [%] [+]` $\rightarrow$ **`\$84.00`**) yields only $\$24 / \$84 = 28.57\%$ margin, whereas dividing cost by the margin complement $\text{Price} = \frac{\text{Cost}}{1 - \text{Margin}}$ via `60 [ENTER] 1 [ENTER] 0.40 [-] [÷]` resolves the true retail price **`\$100.00`**:

| Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | What Happens on the Stack |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| `60 [ENTER] 40 [↱] [%]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 60.00 | 24.00 | 40% markup on \$60.00 cost: \$24.00 |
| `[+]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 84.00 | Flawed markup price: \$84.00 (28.57% margin) |
| `60 [ENTER] 1 [ENTER]` | 84.00 | 60.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | True margin pricing: stage cost \$60 in $Z$ and 1.00 in $Y$ |
| `.40 [-]` | 84.00 | 84.00 | 60.00 | 0.60 | 1 - 0.40 = 0.60 margin complement; \$60.00 drops to $Y$ |
| `[÷]` | 84.00 | 84.00 | 84.00 | 100.00 | True gross margin retail price: \$100.00 |

### 11.4.2 Percent Change (`%CHG`), Cross-Metric Elasticity, CAGR & Inflation

The **Percent Change Function (`[↱] [%CHG]`)** is executed via Right Shift `[↱]` followed by `[%CHG]` using the chronological order **Old Value `[ENTER]` New Value `[↱] [%CHG]`**, preserving the Old Value in Register $Y$ and the New Value in `LASTX`.

Suppose a software company's **Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR)** grew from $\$12.0\text{M}$ to $\$15.6\text{M}$ (`12 [ENTER] 15.6 [↱] [%CHG]` $\rightarrow +30.00\%$), while **Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)** expanded from $\$2.4\text{M}$ to $\$2.88\text{M}$ (`2.4 [ENTER] 2.88 [↱] [%CHG]` $\rightarrow +20.00\%$). Dropping the old baseline out of the way (`[x⇄y] [R↓]`) aligns ARR growth ($Y = 30.00$) and CAC growth ($X = 20.00$) side-by-side on the stack, where pressing `[-]` yields the **`+10.00%`** growth spread and keying `30 [ENTER] 20 [÷]` computes the **`1.5`** growth elasticity multiplier:

| Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | What Happens on the Stack |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| `12 [ENTER] 15.6 [↱] [%CHG]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 12.00 | 30.00 | ARR growth $+30.00\%$ in X; baseline $12.00$ in Y |
| `2.4 [ENTER] 2.88 [↱] [%CHG]` | 12.00 | 30.00 | 2.40 | 20.00 | CAC growth $+20.00\%$ in X; ARR growth lifts to Z |
| `[x⇄y]` | 12.00 | 30.00 | 20.00 | 2.40 | Swap CAC baseline $2.40$ into X |
| `[R↓]` | 2.40 | 12.00 | 30.00 | 20.00 | Roll stack down to align $30.00\%$ in Y and $20.00\%$ in X |
| `[-]` | 2.40 | 2.40 | 12.00 | 10.00 | ARR vs. CAC growth spread $+10.00$ percentage points |

To compute the 5-year **Compound Annual Growth Rate (`CAGR`)** of a venture investment that grows from $\$14.0\text{M}$ to $\$88.5\text{M}$ over $n = 5\text{ years}$ ($\text{CAGR} = (88.5 / 14.0)^{1/5} - 1$), keying `88.5 [ENTER] 14.0 [÷] 5 [1/x] [yˣ] 1 [-] 100 [×]` reveals **`44.60%`**:

| Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | What Happens on the Stack |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| `88.5 [ENTER]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 88.50 | 88.50 | Stage exit valuation $\$88.50\text{M}$ in Register Y |
| `14.0 [÷]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 6.32 | Terminal wealth multiple $88.5 / 14.0 = 6.3214\times$ |
| `5 [1/x]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 6.32 | 0.20 | Reciprocal exponent $1/5 = 0.20$ |
| `[yˣ]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 1.45 | Annualized growth factor $(6.3214)^{0.20} = 1.4460$ |
| `1 [-]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.45 | Deduct unity for decimal growth rate $0.4460$ |
| `100 [×]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 44.60 | Scale to percentage: $\text{CAGR} = 44.60\%/\text{yr}$ |

Conversely, deflating $\$100,000$ of uninvested cash by 20 years of $3.2\%$ annual CPI inflation ($PV = 100,000 / (1.032)^{20}$) via `100000 [ENTER] 1.032 [ENTER] 20 [yˣ] [÷]` reveals that purchasing power erodes to **`53260.60`** ($\mathbf{\$53,260.60}$). ### 11.4.3 The Five-Variable `TVM` Engine: Mortgages, Amortization & Balloon Notes

The onboard **Five-Variable Time Value of Money (`TVM`) Engine** is accessed via Left Shift `[↰]` above `[x∥y]` (Row 7, Column 3):

| TVM Variable | LFU Softkey | Actuarial Description | Computational Units |
| :---: | :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **$N$** | `[N]` (`[LFU0]`) | Total number of compounding periods | Integer or fractional periods |
| **$I\%$** | `[I%YR]` (`[LFU1]`) | Periodic interest rate per compounding period ($i\%$) | Percent per period (e.g. `6.5` for 6.5%/yr or `6.75/12 = 0.5625` for monthly) |
| **$PV$** | `[PV]` (`[LFU2]`) | Present value (initial loan principal or investment) | Currency ($) |
| **$PMT$** | `[PMT]` (`[LFU3]`) | Periodic annuity payment amount | Currency ($ per period) |
| **$FV$** | `[FV]` (`[LFU4]`) | Future value (final balloon balance or accumulated savings) | Currency ($) |
| **Mode** | `END/BEG` (`[LFU5]`) | Payment timing within each period | `END` (Ordinary Annuity) or `BEG` (Annuity Due) |

> **Four Essential `TVM` Rules (`Store-vs.-Solve`, Periodic Rate $i\%$, `END/BEG`, and Persistent Registers):**
> 1. **Store vs. Solve:** Tapping any TVM softkey right after typing or calculating a number on the stack **stores** that value from Register $X$ into the TVM register. Tapping a TVM softkey immediately after another TVM softkey **solves** for that unknown variable into Register $X$.
> 2. **Periodic Interest Rate ($i\%$):** The second TVM softkey (`I%` on `[LFU1]`, denoted `[I%YR]` in keystroke sequences) always stores the **periodic interest rate per compounding period ($i\%$)**. For a monthly mortgage, always divide the annual APR by $12$ (`6.75 [ENTER] 12 [÷]` $\to 0.5625\%$) before tapping the softkey.
> 3. **Ordinary Annuity (`END`) vs. Annuity Due (`BEG`):** Softkey `[LFU5]` (`END/BEG`) toggles directly between **Ordinary Annuity (`END`)**, where payments occur at the *end* of each period (standard for mortgages, auto loans, and bonds), and **Annuity Due (`BEG`)**, where payments occur at the *beginning* of each period (standard for monthly apartment rent, equipment leases, and insurance premiums).
> 4. **Persistent TVM Registers:** Because the five `TVM` registers intentionally retain their stored values across calculations for rapid "what-if" sensitivity analysis, always zero any unused register (such as `0 [FV]` on a fully amortizing loan with no balloon payment, or `[↰] [CLEAR]` $\to$ `[CLVARS]` on `[LFU1]`) before starting a new financial problem!

### 11.4.5 From Single Numbers to the Full Picture

Step back and look at what every calculation across the first eleven chapters of this book has had in common. Whether we solved for the resonant frequency of an AC circuit in Chapter 5, the draft depth of a floating sphere in Chapter 7, a definite Romberg integral in Chapter 8, a Pearson correlation coefficient $r$ in Chapter 9, a 36-bit hexadecimal subnet mask in Chapter 10, or a monthly mortgage payment and internal rate of return in this chapter, **our answer was always a single number at a single point**.

A single high-precision number is indispensable when you already know the shape of the landscape around it. Yet a single number—even when computed to twelve decimal places—is like looking at a mountain range through a pinhole:
* In **root-finding (`SOLVE`)**, a single root $x_1 = 1.42$ cannot tell you at a glance whether the function crosses the horizontal axis a second and third time just a few units to the right, or whether the curve barely grazed the axis near a flat extremum.
* In **physics and financial modeling**, a single cash-flow yield or damping constant cannot show you the visual silhouette of an underdamped suspension ringdown envelope $e^{-\zeta\omega_n t}\cos(\omega_d t)$ or the crossover point where an exponential growth curve overtakes a linear baseline.
* And in **experimental statistics (`L.R.`)**, as Yale statistician Francis Anscombe famously demonstrated in 1973, wildly different scatter patterns can hide behind the exact same summary mean, slope, and correlation coefficient $r$ if you never look at the graph!

How do you step back from a single numerical coordinate and see the **entire behavior of a function or dataset at a single glance** on a pocket screen? And how does a discrete grid of $132 \times 65$ square monochrome pixels transform continuous algebra into smooth geometric curves? That question takes us to a French philosopher's bedroom ceiling in 1637—and to **[Chapter 12: Seeing the Invisible: From Descartes's Bedroom Ceiling to the Pixel Grid](sc32/12-function-scatter-plotting.md)**.

# Chapter 12: Seeing the Invisible: From Descartes's Bedroom Ceiling to the Pixel Grid

## 12.1 The Fly on René Descartes's Ceiling and the Marriage of Algebra and Geometry

### 12.1.1 Morning Meditation at La Flèche: Turning Equations into Curves

As a frail eleven-year-old boarding student at the Jesuit College of La Flèche in Anjou, **René Descartes** was granted an unusual privilege by the rector, Father Charlet: while his classmates rose at five o'clock every morning to recite Latin prayers in unheated stone halls, young René was allowed to remain warm under his blankets until late morning, thinking quietly with his eyes open.

Descartes kept that habit of morning meditation for the rest of his life. According to nineteenth-century mathematical lore, on one such morning as he lay in bed staring up at the corner of his room, a housefly landed on the plastered ceiling and began crawling from tile to tile. Watching the insect wander across the grid, Descartes asked himself how he could tell a friend the exact spot where the fly rested at any instant—and where it was headed next.

Suddenly, the answer flashed before him: if he measured the perpendicular distance $x$ from the left wall and the perpendicular distance $y$ from the back wall, **every position of the fly on the flat ceiling corresponded to a unique pair of numbers $(x, y)$**. Even better, if the fly walked along a straight diagonal line or a smooth circular arc, its two distances $x$ and $y$ obeyed a strict algebraic equation—and conversely, *any* algebraic equation connecting $x$ and $y$ traced a visible geometric curve across the ceiling!

When Descartes published this discovery in **1637** as ***La Géométrie*** *([Descartes, 1637](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-descartes1637))*—an appendix to his *Discourse on the Method*—he ended a two-thousand-year separation that had divided human thought since antiquity:

- **Ancient Greek Geometry (Euclid, Archimedes, Apollonius)** was rich in visual intuition—circles, triangles, parabolas, and tangent lines drawn with straightedge and compass—but it had almost no symbolic algebra. Proving a new theorem required inventing a custom geometric construction from scratch.
- **Medieval & Renaissance Algebra (al-Khwarizmi, Tartaglia, Cardano, Viète)** was a powerful symbolic machine for balancing unknowns ($x^2, x^3$), but it was blind. An equation sat on the page as a dry string of characters with no visual shape.

Descartes proved that **algebra and geometry are two languages describing the exact same reality**. John Stuart Mill later called analytic geometry *"the greatest single step ever made in the progress of the exact sciences,"* because it gave equations **eyes**—and gave geometric shapes **formulas**.

### 12.1.2 Reading the Anatomy of a Curve: Roots, Peaks, Valleys & Inflection Points

Once you translate an algebraic formula $y = f(x)$ into a Cartesian curve across a horizontal $x$-axis (**domain**) and a vertical $y$-axis (**range**)—defined on the SC-32 via the **`[↱] [EQN]`** editor (Right Shift `[↱]` above `[STO]`)—every abstract concept from high-school Algebra II, Precalculus, and introductory calculus turns into an unmistakable landmark on a physical landscape:

1. **Zeros / Roots ($f(x) = 0$ — Where the Curve Crosses Sea Level):**
   In Chapter 7, hunting for the roots of a polynomial or transcendental equation meant searching for values of $x$ where $f(x) = 0$. On a Cartesian graph, a root is simply **a shoreline where the terrain crosses sea level** ($y = 0$), switching from negative elevation ($y < 0$, underwater) to positive elevation ($y > 0$, dry land).
2. **Local Maxima & Minima ($f'(x) = 0$ — Mountain Peaks and Valley Floors):**
   In Chapter 8, we saw that the derivative $f'(x)$ measures the instantaneous slope of a curve. As you hike up a mountain, the slope is positive ($f'(x) > 0$); as you descend the far side, the slope is negative ($f'(x) < 0$). At the exact summit of a smooth hill (**local maximum**) or the bottom of a smooth valley (**local minimum**), the ground beneath your boots is momentarily **flat and horizontal** ($f'(x) = 0$).
3. **Inflection Points ($f''(x) = 0$ — Where the Steering Wheel Passes Through Center):**
   What is an **inflection point**, and how can you feel one in your hands? Imagine driving a car along an S-shaped highway curve modeled by the cubic polynomial:

$$y(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x + 2$$

   Over the first half of the S-curve ($0 \le x < 2$), the road bends clockwise (curving downward on the map, **concave down**, where the second derivative $y''(x) = 6x - 12 < 0$), and your hands hold the steering wheel turned to the right. Over the second half ($2 < x \le 4$), the road bends counterclockwise (**concave up**, $y''(x) > 0$), and your hands hold the steering wheel turned to the left. Right at $x = 2$, where $y''(2) = 6(2) - 12 = 0$ and the road passes through $(2, 4)$, **your steering wheel passes momentarily through dead center** as the curve switches from bending right to bending left.
4. **Vertical & Horizontal Asymptotes (Cliffs and Plateaus):**
   When a rational denominator approaches zero—such as the thin-lens magnification formula $f(x) = \frac{1}{x - 2}$ as an object crosses the focal point $x = 2$—the curve rockets toward $-\infty$ on the left and plunges from $+\infty$ on the right along a **vertical asymptote**. Conversely, when a skydiver steps from a high-altitude balloon under gravity $g$ and quadratic air drag ($v(t) = v_{\text{term}}\tanh(gt/v_{\text{term}})$), or when an uncharged capacitor charges through a resistor toward a supply voltage $V_{\max}$ with RC time constant $\tau$:

$$V(t) = V_{\max}\!\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right)$$

   upward air resistance or capacitor back-voltage gradually balances the driving force, and the curve bends smoothly toward a flat horizontal ceiling—a **horizontal asymptote** at $v = v_{\text{term}}$ or $V = V_{\max}$ as $t \to \infty$.

## 12.2 Rasterization on a Pocket Canvas: Turning Equations into Pixels

### 12.2.1 The Paradox of Digital Graphics: Continuous Math on a Discrete Grid

Descartes imagined his coordinate plane as infinitely smooth: between any two points on a line, there are infinitely many closer points. A computer or calculator screen, however, is **discrete**. Inspect a monochrome liquid-crystal display through a magnifying glass, and you will see a chessboard of tiny rectangular liquid-crystal shutters (**pixels**, short for *picture elements*), each of which is either **ON (dark ink)** or **OFF (reflective paper background)**.

That raises a fascinating computer-science question that bridges Chapter 10 (discrete integer bits) and Chapter 8 (continuous functions): **how does a digital processor translate a smooth, continuous mathematical equation $y = f(x)$ into a crisp ribbon of integer pixels in less than a twentieth of a second?**

Inside the SC-32's $132 \times 65\text{ pixel}$ transflective LCD, the graphical plotting viewport dedicates a clean $128 \times 52\text{ pixel}$ active curve canvas directly above the 13-pixel status and coordinate readout bar. Placing the horizontal domain window $[X_{\min}, X_{\max}]$ into Registers $Y$ and $X$ and pressing **`[↱] [PLOT]`** (Right Shift `[↱]` above `[x∥y]`) launches the firmware's 100-step Bresenham vector renderer across the 128-column plotting canvas in three clean inside-out stages:

### 12.2.2 Stage 1: Slicing the Continuous Domain into Discrete Columns

Suppose you ask the calculator to plot a function $y = f(x)$ across a horizontal world window from $X_{\min} = -3.0$ on the left to $X_{\max} = +3.0$ on the right (a total horizontal span of $\Delta X = X_{\max} - X_{\min} = 6.0$). In firmware, the plotter sweeps $100$ evenly spaced horizontal steps across the 128-column viewport; to illustrate the exact column-sampling algebra on the stack with clean mental fractions, consider a **worked 64-column ($N = 64$, $k = 0, 1, 2, \dots, 63$) affine viewport-mapping benchmark** that divides the span into $N - 1 = 63$ equal steps of width $\Delta x = \frac{X_{\max} - X_{\min}}{63}$:

$$x_k = X_{\min} + k \left(\frac{X_{\max} - X_{\min}}{63}\right), \qquad k = 0, 1, \dots, 63$$

At column $k = 0$ (the left edge), $x_0 = -3.0$; at column $k = 21$ (exact one-third of the way across, since $21 / 63 = 1/3$), $x_{21} = -3.0 + 21 \times \frac{6.0}{63} = -3.0 + 2.0 = -1.0$; and at column $k = 63$ (the right edge), $x_{63} = +3.0$.

### 12.2.3 Stage 2: Auto-Scaling & The Affine Viewport Transformation (Flipping the Y-Axis)

As the calculator evaluates $y_k = f(x_k)$ at each sampled horizontal step across the 128-column canvas, it keeps a running record of the lowest value $Y_{\min} = \min(y_k)$ and the highest value $Y_{\max} = \max(y_k)$—cleverly skipping over any sample where the function hits an undefined division by zero (`NaN` or $\pm\infty$) so a single vertical asymptote does not crush the rest of the graph into a flat line.

Now comes a subtle twist that every game programmer and graphics engineer learns on Day One: **in mathematics, $+y$ points UP, but in computer memory, pixel row numbers $v$ count DOWN from the top-left corner of the screen.**

Within the $132 \times 65$ transflective display's active $128 \times 52\text{ pixel}$ graphing viewport (where horizontal pixel columns run from $u = 0$ on the left to $u = 127$ on the right, and vertical pixel rows run from $v = 0$ at the **top** edge to $v = 51$ at the **bottom** edge above the 13-pixel coordinate readout bar), mapping a continuous world point $(x, y)$ onto an integer screen pixel $(u, v)$ requires a two-step **Affine Viewport Transformation**:

$$u = \left\lfloor \frac{x - X_{\min}}{X_{\max} - X_{\min}} \times 127 \right\rfloor, \qquad v = 51 - \left\lfloor \frac{y - Y_{\min}}{Y_{\max} - Y_{\min}} \times 51 \right\rfloor$$

Examine the inside-out structure of both formulas:
1. **Normalize (`[0, 1]`):** Subtract the minimum bound ($x - X_{\min}$ or $y - Y_{\min}$) and divide by the total window span ($X_{\max} - X_{\min}$ or $Y_{\max} - Y_{\min}$). That turns *any* physical units—whether nanometers of optical wavelength, seconds of rocket burn, or millions of dollars—into a universal dimensionless fraction between $0.0$ and $1.0$.
2. **Scale & Invert:** Multiply the horizontal fraction by $127$ pixels; multiply the vertical fraction by $51$ pixels and subtract from $51$ so the highest mathematical peak ($y = Y_{\max}$) lands at the top row of the screen ($v = 0$) and the lowest valley ($y = Y_{\min}$) lands at the bottom row ($v = 51$).

### 12.2.4 Stage 3: Jack Bresenham's 1962 Integer Line-Drawing Miracle

Wait: if you only light up the isolated sample dots $(u_k, v_k)$ on the screen, a steep curve—like a high-frequency sine wave or a cubic polynomial—will look like a scattered constellation of disconnected dots with wide vertical gaps between columns.

How do you connect two pixel coordinates $(u_0, v_0)$ and $(u_1, v_1)$ with a continuous, gap-free straight line segment on a square grid?

In **1962**, a twenty-four-year-old engineer named **Jack Elton Bresenham** was working at IBM's computation laboratory in San Jose, California. He wanted to write a program to drive an early CalComp mechanical drum plotter attached to an IBM 1401 computer. There was just one catch: the computer had **no floating-point hardware** and **no fast division instruction**. If the plotter had to compute a floating-point slope $m = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta u}$ and round decimals at every single pixel step, drawing one graph would take forever.

Bresenham asked a brilliant inside-out question: suppose we are drawing a line that moves $\Delta u = u_1 - u_0$ pixels to the right and rises $\Delta v = |v_1 - v_0|$ pixels vertically (with $\Delta v \le \Delta u$, and swapping the roles of $u$ and $v$ whenever a steep curve segment rises faster than it runs, $\Delta v > \Delta u$). As we step one column to the right ($u \leftarrow u + 1$), the true mathematical line rises by the fraction $\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta u}$ of a pixel. We only need to decide a simple binary question: **is the true line closer to staying on the current pixel row $v$, or stepping one pixel row up ($v \pm 1$)?**

Instead of dividing $\Delta v$ by $\Delta u$ and comparing the fraction against $\frac{1}{2}$ ($0.5$), Bresenham multiplied the entire inequality by $2\Delta u$ to clear the fraction completely. That left an **integer error accumulator**:

$$\epsilon_0 = 2\Delta v - \Delta u$$

- On each horizontal pixel step, if $\epsilon < 0$, the line has not yet crossed the halfway mark: stay on the same row $v$ and add $2\Delta v$ to $\epsilon$.
- If $\epsilon \ge 0$, the line has crossed the halfway mark: step one pixel vertically ($v \leftarrow v \pm 1$) and add $2(\Delta v - \Delta u)$ to $\epsilon$.

Zero fractions, zero floating-point decimals, and zero divisions—just integer addition, subtraction, and a bit-shift by $2$! **Bresenham's Line Algorithm** became one of the foundational pillars of computer graphics, etched into the silicon of every modern graphics card, laser printer, CNC milling controller, and the SC-32's 42-millisecond vector plotting engine *([HP, 1991](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-hp32sii1991))*.
